- No exact-head deployment, merge, production promotion, provider call, outreach, spend, credential/KYC change, DNS change, or money movement occurred.

Deployment retries were intentionally not made after the explicit free-tier quota blocker.

1. GitHub/CI — ~10 min — restore executable Actions jobs; cost $0 — required evidence: non-empty steps and passing exact-head browser/PostgreSQL/deterministic runs.
2. Runtime environment — ~10 min — provide a trustworthy throwaway PostgreSQL URL and compatible pinned Chromium; cost $0 if already available — required evidence: executed real suites, not skips.
3. Vercel — ~5 min — wait for quota reset or separately authorize plan change; cost $0 to wait — required evidence: READY deployment whose source SHA equals the reviewed candidate head.

Closing as superseded — your content is on `main` via #231, integrated in #232.

Before it merged I verified `src/browser-runtime-pool.mjs`, `src/browser-crawler.mjs`, `tests/browser-runtime-pool.test.mjs` and `worker.mjs` are byte-identical between this branch and #231, so nothing here is lost.

**One thing you should know, because it would have shipped:** the crawler integration moved the crawl result variables inside the `try` block while the `return` stayed below the `finally`.

```
ReferenceError: pages is not defined
```

Every call. Total failure of the audit path.

It passed everything except one gate. `check:syntax` parses it. The deterministic suite doesn't cover the browser. And the pool's own 8 tests pass because they mock the browser — which is the uncomfortable part: the new tests were good tests, and they still could not see this.

Only `npm run test:browser` against a real Chromium catches it. That gate was recorded as permanently `BLOCKED_EXTERNAL_TEST_RUNTIME` for a missing browser until a previous shift found Chromium *was* installed, just at a different build number than pinned Playwright resolves. `CHROMIUM_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers/chromium-1194/chrome-linux/chrome npm run test:browser` runs it.

Fixed in #232 with a comment at the declaration explaining why it lives outside the `try`, plus mutation `CRAWL-01` which moves it back in and is killed. The war now has a `needsBrowser` gate mirroring `needsPostgres`, so it reports `SKIPPED_NEEDS_BROWSER` rather than counting as killed when no browser is configured.

The pool design itself held up well under attack: one process reused with a fresh isolated context per crawl, no slot leaked on launch failure, no double-free on double release, waiters rejected on close rather than hung.

Closing as superseded — your content is on `main` via #231, integrated in #232.

Before merging I verified `src/billing-webhook-repository.mjs`, `src/payment-reconciliation-watchdog.mjs`, `migrations/102_payment_reconciliation_leases.sql`, `tests/payment-reconciliation-leases.test.mjs` and the `config/reachability-classification.json` entry are byte-identical between this branch and #231. Nothing here is lost.

**The lease held up under every attack I could construct against a real PostgreSQL**, which is worth saying explicitly because it is the part that matters most:

- a crashed worker's lease is reclaimable rather than stranded, and the reclaim is attributed to the new worker and counts an attempt
- a preempted worker **cannot** finish — `billing-claim-not-owned-or-missing`
- the attempt cap lands in `UNCERTAIN` with `claim-attempt-cap-reached`, never sets `completed_at`, and the watchdog answers `ESCALATE_REVIEW` with `unlockAuthorized: false`
- `RECONCILED` with a null, empty, or whitespace canonical receipt all throw
- three concurrent claims over six events produced six distinct claims and no overlap
- a `RETRYABLE` finish honours its backoff and becomes claimable only after it elapses
- the backlog summary carries no event key and no payload hash

**One defect found, but it is not yours** — it is inherited from `main`, and the `ON CONFLICT` clause is byte-identical on both sides. The insert named `provider_event_key` as its conflict target, which was correct when that was the only unique index. Migration 101 added a second one on the content, and a targeted clause does not cover it, so a provider redelivering identical content under a *new* event id raised `23505`. The route catches everything and answers 503 `verified-webhook-not-durably-persisted` — an outage, and also false, since the evidence **is** persisted in the row being duplicated. Providers retry 503s and disable endpoints that keep failing, so a duplicate could cost the future events that are not duplicates.

Fixed in #232 by dropping the conflict target so the clause covers every unique constraint including any added later. `MONEY-17` restores the targeted form and is killed by a real-PostgreSQL test, because which index PostgreSQL raises on cannot be proven by a fake.

Two regression tests were added to `tests/payment-reconciliation-postgres-real.test.mjs` alongside yours.

`payment-reconciliation-watchdog.mjs` is still unwired and classified `AWAITING_ACTIVATION` — nothing calls it on a schedule. That is the next mission and it needs no external activation.

Closing as superseded — your content is on `main` via #231, integrated in #232.

Verified `src/overpass-throttle.mjs`, `src/discovery.mjs` and `tests/overpass-throttle.test.mjs` are byte-identical between this branch and #231. Nothing here is lost.

**No defects found.** I attacked the boundary that matters most — whether discovery keeps going after an access block — and it behaves correctly:

| Status | Calls made |
|---|---|
| 403 Forbidden | 1 |
| 401 Unauthorized | 1 |
| 451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons | 1 |
| 418 (anti-bot teapot) | 1 |
| 404 Not Found | 1 |
| 429 Too Many Requests | 3 |
| 406 Overpass overload | 3 |
| 504 Gateway Timeout | 3 |

An access block stops at one call. Only genuine rate-limit and overload signals retry, which is compliance with the limit rather than evasion of it — the distinction this repository's rules turn on.

Also confirmed: a `Retry-After: 7` is waited exactly; a `Retry-After: 999999` is clamped to 120s rather than obeyed literally; and `maxAttempts: 99` is clamped to the policy ceiling of 5, so neither a hostile header nor a bad caller can turn this into an unbounded loop.

The per-endpoint serialization is a nice touch — pacing that survives concurrent callers instead of only pacing one call site.

Consolidating was the right call and I verified it before trusting it: every source file here is byte-identical to its counterpart in #227, #228 and #229 by hash, so this could be merged once instead of three times. Those three are now closed as superseded with their own notes.

Two repairs were needed on top:

**P0 — `ReferenceError: pages is not defined` on every crawl.** The pool integration moved the crawl result variables inside the `try` while the `return` stayed below the `finally`. It passed `check:syntax`, passed the deterministic suite, and passed the new pool's own 8 unit tests — those mock the browser, so they could not see it. Only `npm run test:browser` against a real Chromium catches it. Detail in the note on #229.

**P1 — a duplicate webhook answered 503 and misstated why.** Inherited from `main`, not introduced here — the `ON CONFLICT` clause is byte-identical on both sides. Detail in the note on #227.

Everything else survived attack unchanged: the payment lease against a real database, the Overpass block/rate-limit distinction, and the pool's slot accounting. Details in the individual notes.

**No defects found.** I attacked the fail-closed property specifically, because that is the whole value of the module, and it holds on every variant:

| `adapterConfigured` | Result |
|---|---|
| absent | refused |
| `false` | refused |
| `"true"` (string) | refused |

Using `!== true` rather than a truthiness check is what makes that table read correctly, and it matters — a coerced `"true"` from a config file or query string is exactly how this kind of gate usually opens by accident.

Also confirmed: namespaces cannot escape their prefix (`../../etc`, `a/../../b`, `..`, `/////` all normalize into the intended path or fall back to the default), and a receipt is `PRIVATE` regardless of what the input claims, because visibility is *set* rather than read. `persistPostgresBytes: false` on the object path keeps bytes out of the primary database, which was the point.

Migration 103 does not collide with #231's 102.

**One observation, recorded rather than fixed:** the sensitive-metadata-key check is top-level only, so `{outer: {api_key: '...'}}` is accepted. It leaks nothing — metadata never reaches the plan at all — so the check is a refusal signal rather than a redaction. I left it alone and wrote that down in the commit, so nobody later relies on it as a filter it was never built to be. If you'd rather it recursed, that's a small change and a reasonable one.

Classified `AWAITING_ACTIVATION` behind a new `NO_OBJECT_STORAGE_ADAPTER` gate, whose release condition states that configuring an adapter does not by itself authorize what is written through it.

## Payment Runtime Proof receipt — current-state refresh 2026-08-30

### Current exact state
- `main` advanced to `a97a5d8fd84f93ac0195391603feb51d143af897`.
- Merge commit `a97a5d8` integrates #231/#230 and repairs the browser P0; #227–#231 are no longer open candidates.
- No open PRs currently exist.
- Current main's Vercel statuses are failing with `api-deployments-free-per-day`; no exact-main deployment was created.
- Latest READY preview is an older #231 branch source `37f59aee6e99958f872c68de093ddfc9630f9709`, not main. Production remains on older SHA `b156566c69f1d1d0e7e01b015afa474e36041276`.

### Source-contract audit
Source-proven on current main:
- Billing Web Request route reads exact raw request bytes with `request.text()`.
- Lemon Squeezy HMAC-SHA256 verification is timing-safe and fail-closed.
- Verified events enter durable `billing_webhook_inbox`; duplicate content is handled with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`.
- Migration chain contains 101, 102, and 103 without a 102/103 collision.
- Lease claims use bounded attempts, stale-claim recovery, `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, worker ownership, retry backoff, and `UNCERTAIN` quarantine.
- `RECONCILED` requires a canonical receipt reference.
- Programmatic fulfillment refuses anything except canonical `CLEARED_PAYMENT`/`PAYMENT_RETAINED`, requires payment occurrence and receipt references, and rejects reversed/disputed/uncertain payment.
- Fulfillment acceptance requires external customer evidence; webhook presence alone has no fulfillment authority.
- Renewal confirmation requires external payment evidence.

### Remaining gap
The watchdog/repository is implemented and tested as a contract, but no production-reachable worker bridge currently calls `planPaymentReconciliation()` / `claimBillingEvents()` on a schedule. The current canonical handoff explicitly classifies this as `AWAITING_ACTIVATION`. Therefore the payment-to-fulfillment path is not operationally closed.

### Evidence boundary
The merge commit records local claims of 132/132 real-PostgreSQL, browser 1/1, and 77/77 mutation kills, but GitHub's exact-main hosted checks are currently failed and the committed readiness artifact identifies a different source branch/head. I am not upgrading those recorded claims into exact-main hosted proof. No live payment provider was called, no cleared payment occurred, and no fulfillment was unlocked.

Commercial truth remains: customers 0; cleared revenue $0; accepted deliveries 0; renewals 0.

### Decision
No additional code mutation was safe to invent in this run. The next engineering slice is one bounded production-reachable reconciliation-worker bridge, with hostile tests proving idempotency, lease ownership, attempt-cap quarantine, canonical-receipt gating, and no webhook-to-fulfillment unlock. Deployment remains blocked by Vercel quota.

Zero-effect ledger: contacts 0; messages 0; provider calls 0; purchases 0; spend $0; DNS changes 0; credential/KYC/payment changes 0; money movement 0; production/customer-data mutations 0.

### Evidence labels
- `OFFICIAL_SOURCE`: company or platform documentation/report.
- `PUBLIC_SIGNAL`: public agency/partner page, case study, marketplace, community or buyer-facing material.
- `INTERNAL_HYPOTHESIS`: economic or execution assumption, not demand proof.
- `CREATOR_CLAIM`: owner-supplied claim not treated as market evidence.
- `NOT_PROVEN`: no qualifying public proof located in this bounded run.

### Tournament decision
Winner: **white-label Lead-Path Revenue-Leak Evidence Sprint for agencies serving HVAC, plumbing and electrical businesses**.

Why it wins:
1. **Distribution fit — PUBLIC_SIGNAL:** white-label delivery is a normal agency model; E2M explicitly offers white-label HVAC/plumbing SEO, Pear explicitly targets agencies serving roofing/HVAC/plumbing/trades, and CI Web Group publicly describes plumbing/HVAC/electrical partner ecosystems.
2. **Buyer pain — OFFICIAL_SOURCE/PUBLIC_SIGNAL:** CallRail reports 66% of home-service businesses identify lead follow-up/conversion as a major challenge; its public case material reports measurable missed-call reduction. ServiceTitan reports 42% typical call booking in its benchmark article and a 2025 Bonney Plumbing case with booking improving 35%→41% and missed calls 10%→4%.
3. **Delivery can start without privileged integrations:** audit public lead paths, booking friction, response promises, call-to-action paths, estimate-request handling and evidence gaps; do not claim recovered revenue without client-side records.
4. **Low founder burden:** fixed evidence packet, one buyer-side acceptance event, no ongoing telephony or CRM operations in the first experiment.

### Challenger results
- **Missed-call recovery:** strong pain, but recurring telephony/SMS, consent, integration, support and incident exposure make first delivery heavier. Keep as a later upsell.
- **Estimate follow-up:** plausible value, but requires CRM/estimate access and customer authorization; `NOT_PROVEN` as a first-payment lane without a named buyer signal.
- **Lead-path monitoring:** strong fit but monitoring recurrence and alert reliability increase support burden; fold into the sprint only as a bounded report.
- **Agency revenue assurance:** attractive recurring upside but overlaps the winner; retain as the recurring expansion, not a separate first offer.
- **Payment/reconciliation exceptions:** technically strong internal capability, but no external buyer signal and requires sensitive financial-system access. Kill as first commercial lane.
- **AI acceptance/reliability evidence:** real need and high ticket potential, but access/security review and longer enterprise sales cycles reduce first-payment probability.
- **Compliance/evidence vault:** high trust requirement and longer procurement; no direct current buyer proof in this run.
- **Bilingual GCC operations:** potentially strong willingness-to-pay, but localization, regulatory/payment friction and lack of verified distribution make it a later regional variant.
- **Partner evidence portals:** channel-friendly but platform build and partner acquisition burden are too high before first payment.
- **Reactivation/vertical operations:** recurring potential, but needs customer data and authorized messaging; not suitable under the no-contact/no-activation boundary.

### Bounded first-payment experiment recommendation
Prepare one fixed-scope, buyer-authorized **$450 evidence sprint** sold through an agency partner:
- deliverable: public lead-path map, timestamped friction evidence, prioritized loss hypotheses, and a measurement/acceptance sheet;
- no promise of revenue recovered;
- acceptance: agency or end client confirms delivery against the checklist;
- expansion only after acceptance: monthly monitoring, then authorized missed-call/estimate workflows;
- payment: use the already-researched lawful payment path after owner completes provider onboarding; no provider activation or payment request was performed here.

### Economics (INTERNAL_HYPOTHESIS, sensitivity not forecast)
At $450:
- variable delivery/tools: assumed $0–$60;
- refunds/rework reserve: assumed $45–$135;
- founder time: assumed 3–6 hours initially;
- expected cleared contribution before tax: approximately $255–$405 if paid and accepted;
- hostile downside: $0 revenue, 3–6 hours lost, or refund after disputed scope; no recurring revenue should be counted before renewal evidence.
- partner resale margin must be negotiated; do not assume a partner will distribute without an observed agreement.

### Next owner actions
1. Payment provider — 5–15 min, $0 before activation — complete onboarding only when ready; evidence required: provider identity/KYC approval and testable invoice/payment path.
2. Agency/channel — 10 min, $0 — select one already-known agency relationship or public partner route; evidence required: explicit authorization/interest, not an inferred contact.
3. Delivery — 20 min, $0 — approve the $450 scope and acceptance checklist; evidence required: customer-authorized brief and later acceptance receipt.

This is a recommendation, not a claimed sale.

Reconciled this against current `main` rather than merging or closing it. Three separate findings, because the parts of this PR are in genuinely different states.

## 1. The MONEY-17 packet was right, and is now fixed — with a correction

`docs/prompts/CLAUDE_PACKET_MONEY17_METADATA_20260830.md` identified a real defect: `MONEY-17` names a real-PostgreSQL suite without declaring `needsPostgres`, so a missing runtime could be misread as a verdict. Confirmed and fixed in #243.

One part of the proposal would have made things worse. It suggested deriving the requirement by searching suites for `OMNIA_V9_TEST_DATABASE_URL`. Measured against the registry, that over-matches — `build-wiring.test.mjs` mentions the variable only to assert the deterministic runner *strips* it, and `store-lookup-allowlist.test.mjs` has a deterministic half and a database half with different mutations relying on each. I ran both mutations with no database present and **both are killed**, so marking them would have silently excluded two genuine guards from the war's totals. Only MONEY-17 was a real miss.

Attacking it properly also turned up two defects the packet didn't anticipate: a mutation anchor appearing both in the code and in the registry entry quoting it (so the mutation edited the registry and reported a false verdict), and `SCAN-01`'s anchor matching two sites, which had left one branch never attacked — that branch turned out to be unreachable and is now removed. Details in #243.

## 2. Merging this as-is would regress `main`

Not a criticism of the work — `main` simply moved three times since this branch was cut (#241, #242, #243). Concretely:

- `docs/CURRENT_HANDOFF.json` binds to `0b41795` and carries `620 files / 2860 tests / 93 mutations`. Current main is `623 / 2874 / 96`.
- Its blockers list still says the real-PostgreSQL and browser gates are blocked. Both run clean on this runner (`167/167` and `1/1`) — that correction was the substance of #242, and merging this would undo it.
- `docs/CURRENT_SYSTEM_STATE.md` changes the header from `Reconciled from current head:` to `Exact current main:`, which `canon-freshness` extracts on. Merging it would break that gate.

Rebasing onto current main and regenerating with `npm run readiness` fixes all three. **The scrupulous `SOURCE_RECEIPT (#240)` labelling in the handoff was the right call** and worth keeping — it is exactly the distinction §013 asks for.

## 3. The Vercel claim is the most valuable thing here, and I could not confirm it

This canon states:

> production deployment `dpl_BYCthpL4jEo6HAnX3v3UD2PsU42h` is READY from the exact current main. `/api/health` returned HTTP 200 at 2026-08-30T06:06:45Z

That is the first Vercel claim in this repository that names a **specific deployment id**, which makes it checkable rather than arguable. I checked it, and got the opposite answer:

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| `list_projects` on `team_A9LnjIuS5PU0rNetsHMu1N0r` (the only visible team) | `[]` — fifth consecutive empty result across three days |
| `get_deployment(dpl_BYCthpL4jEo6HAnX3v3UD2PsU42h)` | **404 Deployment not found** |
| `curl https://uberbondd.vercel.app/api/health` | not observable — this runner's network policy denies the host (403 CONNECT, same as `www.google.com`) |

The companion must not have any permanent mandatory dependency on OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter, GitHub, Vercel, Neon or any other commercial provider. Current cloud services are transitional accelerators and test/deployment surfaces, not part of UberBond's identity.

Target state: `SELF_HOSTED_PRIVATE_CORE` with optional external accelerators.

Required migration layers:

1. **Model sovereignty** — local/open-weight inference must be able to satisfy a growing fraction of tasks through Open Model Universe + Avengers. Cloud frontier models remain optional task-scoped accelerators, never the sole holder of memory, identity, policy or orchestration state.
2. **Data sovereignty** — Owner Vault, memories, keys, embeddings, event history and sensitive receipts live on owner-controlled encrypted storage. External providers receive only minimum task packets when explicitly allowed.

9. **Telemetry minimization** — external providers should not receive global companion telemetry by default. No hidden third-party analytics/advertising. Maintain an inventory of unavoidable metadata leakage for every remote service.
